analysis.one_liner: Requires above-ground oil and chemical storage tanks to have certified spill-prevention systems and makes owners pay to clean up leaks.
analysis.headline: The Tank Spill Prevention Act died in committee: the House Energy and Commerce Committee held hearings in July 1989 but never voted, and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created the first federal rules for above-ground storage tanks holding oil and hazardous substances. Owners would have to install containment systems big enough to catch a full tank's worth of spilled material, file engineer-certified spill-prevention plans, carry financial backing for cleanup, and pay for damages — including harm to natural resources — when their tanks leak. The bill never got a vote: after hearings in July 1989, it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or draw drinking water near above-ground storage tanks holding oil and hazardous substances, and the local governments that would have to respond to spills. The bill would have required each tank to have a certified spill-prevention system able to catch and hold 110 percent of its contents, a site-specific prevention plan with trained response personnel and prompt notification of authorities, and made owners strictly liable for cleanup costs, property damage, and harm to natural resources [S2][S3]. State environmental agencies also gain: they could take over enforcement with EPA approval, and grants from a new fee-funded Tank Spill Enforcement Fund would pay for administering state programs [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near fuel and chemical tanks

how_it_helps.text: Requires each above-ground tank to have a spill and leak prevention system able to catch and hold 110 percent of the tank's full capacity, with secondary containment for the entire contents, so a tank failure does not spread contamination beyond the operator's property into soil, surface water, or groundwater

Requires a spill-prevention plan written for each specific facility, with trained response personnel, periodic tank testing, prompt notification of the National Response Center and the nearest local government, and certification by an independent professional engineer

Lets the EPA require corrective action after any release and shut down a facility until the problem is fixed, including providing alternative water supplies and water treatment for affected communities; if the owner will not act, the EPA can clean up itself and bill the owner

Makes tank owners strictly liable for cleanup costs, property damage, lost profits of people who depend on affected resources, and harm to natural resources, with government trustees empowered to recover damages for the public and spend them restoring the damaged resources
Funds state enforcement through a fee on tank owners rather than general taxpayers, and lets states take over enforcement so long as their rules are at least as strict as the federal ones

Backs the requirements with real teeth: civil penalties up to $10,000 per tank per day of violation, up to $25,000 per day for defying an EPA order, and criminal penalties of up to five years in prison for knowing violations that cause a release

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of above-ground storage tanks — mainly oil, petrochemical, and industrial companies — would bear the cost: building containment systems large enough to hold 110 percent of tank capacity, hiring independent engineers to certify plans and systems, paying a per-tank fee to fund enforcement, carrying financial-resistance coverage (insurance, bonds, or letters of credit), and paying strict liability for cleanup costs, property damage, and natural resource damages after any release [S2][S3]. Some of these costs would likely be passed through to consumers in fuel and chemical prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be expensive: secondary containment sized to 110 percent of tank capacity plus independent engineer certification would fall hardest on smaller operators, and tank owners would likely pass much of the cost to consumers through higher fuel and chemical prices
The bill would have imposed a new per-tank fee on all above-ground tanks to fund administration, an ongoing cost layered on top of construction and insurance requirements

The bill let the EPA set limits on total liability per incident, a concession to tank owners that could cap what spill victims recover unless the spill involved gross negligence, a regulation violation, or a failure to report or cooperate

The EPA already had some spill-prevention authority over oil storage under existing water-pollution law, so critics could argue the bill layered a parallel program and certification bureaucracy on top of requirements that partially overlapped

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits were substantial and concrete: certified containment that stops a tank failure from reaching groundwater and waterways, guaranteed response capacity and notification, and strict liability that puts cleanup and restoration costs on the companies whose tanks leak rather than on taxpayers and affected communities. The costs — containment construction, engineer certification, insurance, fees, and liability exposure — were real but were concentrated on the tank-owning industry, with some pass-through to consumer prices, and the bill cushioned small tanks with exemptions for tanks of 4,200 gallons or less and farm and residential tanks [S3]. The design was reasonably balanced, including state delegation, fee-funded administration, and preserved state authority to go further. The bill's main problem was not its content but its fate: with only two cosponsors and no committee action after the hearings, it never got the floor test its subject matter might have warranted.

outcome.mechanism: The House Energy and Commerce Committee held hearings in July 1989 but never approved the bill, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Doug Walgren introduced the bill on April 13, 1989, with two cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials on May 1, 1989, which held a hearing on July 12; the full committee held a hearing the next day, July 13
No further action was ever recorded: the committee never marked up or approved the bill, and the House never voted on it
The bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, with no counterpart Senate action recorded

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and operators of above-ground storage tanks — chiefly oil, petrochemical, and industrial companies — came out ahead: they avoided the containment, certification, insurance, fee, and liability costs the bill would have imposed. Communities near tank farms kept the existing, weaker regime, in which federal rules specifically covered underground but not above-ground tanks.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no votes and no recorded opposition: only 2 of 257 House Democrats cosponsored, and the bill died in committee without either party taking a position on the floor.

industries.industry: Owners and operators of above-ground storage tanks (petroleum and chemical storage)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed its core costs directly on these companies: certified containment systems holding 110 percent of tank capacity, engineer-certified prevention plans, per-tank fees funding enforcement, required financial backing, and strict liability for cleanup and natural resource damages after a release [S2][S3]. Defeating the bill preserved the status quo, in which federal tank rules targeted underground tanks while above-ground tanks faced weaker requirements.

The bill required every tank's spill-prevention plan and system to be certified by an independent professional engineer and updated as new technology developed, creating a recurring stream of paid inspection and certification work [S2][S3].

The bill required owners to demonstrate financial responsibility through insurance, guarantees, surety bonds, or letters of credit, creating new demand for these products, while the direct claims-against-guarantor provision and liability terms added underwriting exposure for the firms providing that backing [S3].
